articles.title: Pig kidney works for a record 271 days inside the body of American patient
articles.summary: A New Hampshire man, at death’s door 1 ½ years ago, said Friday he could now have “decades” left after surviving a record 271 days with a transplanted pig kidney — in a procedure that could offer new hope to countless other patients.
articles.body: A New Hampshire man, at death’s door 1 ½ years ago, said Friday he could now have “decades” left after surviving a record 271 days with a transplanted pig kidney — in a procedure that could offer new hope to countless other patients. When Tim Andrews and doctors first started discussing a pig transplant in late 2024, the patient with end-stage kidney failure said he was convinced death was near. But Andrews, 68, wanted to try this procedure, if just for the findings and data it could yield for researchers. “I didn’t think I was going to live through it, to be honest. But I wanted to do it for humanity,” he told NBC News on Friday. “I realized, OK, I’m a dead man. I’m a dead man walking. So I said to myself, ‘What have I done? What have I done with my life? This is an opportunity for me to do something that most people don’t get an opportunity to do, and that’s to help humanity.’” He added that as he discussed the procedure with Dr. Leonardo Riella, he told him, ‘”this is about learning something. I don’t care if I die, as long as you learn one thing (from this procedure).’ ” Andrews’ treatment at Mass General Brigham in Boston marked a significant step forward in xenotransplantation, the transplantation of living organs from one species into another, according to findings published Thursday in The Lancet medical journal. Andrews, a retired grocery store manager from Barrington New Hampshire, was 66 when he received the pig kidney on Jan. 25, 2025. The case shows that a transplanted pig kidney can safely support renal function “while also serving as a bridge” to a subsequent transplant with a human kidney, the study authors wrote. Over the following 271 days he needed no dialysis before receiving a human transplant, according to a statement from Mass General. “His case represents the longest dialysis-free survival following porcine kidney xenotransplantation in a living human and the first transition to human kidney transplantation,” the hospital said. Andrews has reacted well to receiving a human donor kidney. “We could be talking decades (of life expectancy),” said the father of three children between the ages of 40 to 46. “It’s running perfect. I mean, the thing is perfect.” The past few years have given him new appreciation for the “little things in life.” He now relishes daily acts of smelling flowers, swimming, riding a bike and fishing. “Every day I wake up. I’m like, (this is) another (extra) day because I should have been dead a year ago or more,” Andrews said. The patient knows nothing about the kidney donor, other than he was a young man who enjoyed blueberries — a fruit Andrews didn’t care much for in his first six decades of life, but now has developed a strange affinity for. “To know that somebody died way younger and I’m living because of it, that’s pretty tough,” said an emotional Andrews, his voice trailing off. “I have this new kidney in me and I need to honor it.” Xenotransplantation could soon become a lifesaving option, according to Riella, the study’s lead author. “The organ shortage is the greatest crisis we have right now in transplantation,” wrote Riella. “We know that the best treatment option for patients with end-stage kidney disease who have developed renal failure is transplantation, but we simply don’t have enough human organs to transplant in a timely manner.” More than 100,000 people are on the national transplant waiting list. The vast majority are waiting for a kidney. Towana Looney lived with a pig kidney for a then-record 130 days before it was removed in April 2025 because her body began rejecting it. The 55-year-old is still alive and on dialysis in the hopes of finding a matching human donor, a representative for NYU Langone Health said Friday. For patients like Andrews, using pig kidneys could help buy them enough time to find a human donor. “Our vision is that xenotransplantation could help address this gap — initially as a bridge to get patients off dialysis while they wait for a human donor kidney, and potentially, as we establish long-term safety and durability, as a destination therapy in its own right,” Riella said. There could be a day in the near future when pig kidney transplants could be regularly used as a bridge to human donors. “When we talked the first time and I met Dr. Riella, they were talking about at least 10 years, that it’s going to be at least 10 years before this becomes viable — now they’re talking about five years or less than five years,” Andrews said, adding he “may live to see it” become a common procedure. Mass General performed the world’s first pig-to-human kidney transplant in 2024. Richard “Rick” Slayman lived for 52 days before dying of cardiac causes unrelated to the transplant, the hospital said. “I read about it and they told me he died, but he died of other causes, the kidney was still working,” Andrews said. “I said, ‘Huh, you know what? I think this might work.’ ”

articles.title: Oman says no to Iranian toll plan for Strait of Hormuz: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Oman has rejected an Iranian proposal to impose fees on commercial vessels using the Strait of Hormuz, despite an earlier claim by Iran’s Islamic Revo.
articles.body: Oman has rejected an Iranian proposal to impose fees on commercial vessels using the Strait of Hormuz, despite an earlier claim by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that the two countries had reached an agreement on sharing revenue from the strategic waterway, according to a New York Post report.A senior regional official told the New York Post that Oman had declined to approve the proposed charges, including fees that would have been collected voluntarily for environmental and security services.The development appears to contradict a statement made previously by an IRGC spokesman, who said agreements had been reached on the two countries’ respective shares of the waterway and its revenues. A US official had previously told the NY Post that the terms of any revenue-sharing arrangement had not even been finalised by Tehran.The Strait of Hormuz, which lies between Iran and Oman, is a crucial route for global oil and gas shipments. Iran has been seeking greater control over arrangements governing the waterway, including a framework that would give it a larger role after the ongoing conflict.Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi and Omani foreign minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi discussed the strait during a meeting in Tehran last week. Hours later, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi announced that an agreement had been reached on revenue sharing.Oman’s decision also helps it avoid a direct confrontation with US President Donald Trump, who has threatened military action if Muscat interferes with the US position on the waterway. Trump had warned on August 17 that the US would bomb Oman if it obstructed American efforts involving the strait.Any Iranian-Omani agreement on tolls would also face a practical obstacle because the US has reimposed a naval blockade of Iran, meaning a fee-collection arrangement would be difficult to implement without Washington's consent, according to the Post.Oman has maintained close ties with the United States while also serving as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran. The Gulf state previously hosted US-Iran nuclear talks and helped broker a May 2025 ceasefire between the US and Iran-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.The New York Post reported that Oman is now backing away from the Iranian proposal as it seeks to support wider diplomatic efforts.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Rob Brydon 'regrets' turning down Dolly Parton interview
articles.summary: The comedian visited Dollywood in his BBC series Rob Brydon's Honky Tonk road trip.
articles.body:
Gavin and Stacey star Rob Brydon says he "regrets" turning down the chance to interview Dolly Parton after choosing to stay on a family holiday.

Brydon fronted the BBC documentary series Honky Tonk Road Trip, where he travelled across the American South to celebrate 100 years of country music.

In it he visited Dollywood, a theme park created by Parton, where Dolly's relatives had traced the lineage of the Parton and Owens sides to Wales .

He was told he could interview Parton if he returned after filming had ended, but chose to stay on his family holiday in Arizona - an opportunity he now wished he had taken because he never got to meet her before she died.

Parton died peacefully in hospital in Nashville on 25 August following a brief battle with cancer. She was admitted to hospital four days before her death with kidney and autoimmune issues.

"I sort of regret it now," he told Lucy Owen during an interview on BBC Radio Wales .

"I kind of wish that I had gone back because I never met her."

During the interview, Owen compared Brydon "encouraging children to pick up a book" with Parton's dedication to support children through literacy with her Imagination Library scheme.

The global book-gifting scheme delivers one free book every month to children from birth until they turn five years old.

Owen told him that it felt "like a really lovely circle".

"That hadn't occurred to me, but yeah, you're right," Brydon said.

The Welsh actor and comedian's debut children's book - The Cat in The Cupboard - will be published on 10 September.

Aimed at children aged between five and seven, the tale was inspired by the stories he invented for his children about their own ginger cat.

Brydon said he had long made up stories and songs "for my own enjoyment" and was excited to share this with others.

The story, which is told entirely in rhyme, follows Crumble the cat on his daring garden adventures.

He explained the idea came when they had to move their cat flap and "it went to the corner of the house... which meant that he came into the house via a cupboard".

"I just remember saying, 'Oh, the cat in the cupboard, the cat in the cupboard, that sounds nice'," he said.

The father of five said he had "a ridiculous number of children", ranging in age from 15 to 32, and had plenty of experience of reading to them over the years, which helped shape his book.

He said the book was influenced by classics, adding: "One of the only poems I can recite is The Owl and the Pussycat and I suppose there's a similar metre to that."

Brydon has also been praised by teachers for not being afraid to introduce children to unfamiliar words, such as the use of "irascible" to describe the cat's grumpy neighbour.

He added: "I just wanted everyone to be able to read it to their children."

Brydon also spoke about another writing duo he admires - his fellow Gavin and Stacey cast mates Ruth Jones and James Corden.

He shared that he "can't wait" to see their new comedy project, The Choir , adding: "They have a kind of magic when they write together."

But said he doesn't "know if any of our crowd are in it".

However, he told eager listeners that the cast are "still very much in touch" via their "active WhatsApp group".

"It was Alison's birthday the other day and there was a flurry of activity then," he said.

articles.title: Cellist Jacqueline du Pre's belongings fetch £52k at auction
articles.summary: This was the first of two auctions of the cellist's "incredibly personal" belongings.
articles.body:
A collection of items belonging to the renowned cellist Jaquelin du Pre has sold for just under £52,000 at auction.

The collection featured 137 lots from du Pre's childhood and early career, and went under the hammer at Gardiner Houlgate auctions in Corsham, Wiltshire, on Friday.

Handwritten letters, photographs and sheet music were all sold to buyers from as far away as the US and Europe.

"The upper estimate would have been £35,000 or £40,000, so it's well exceeded the upper estimate," said Jamie South, director at Gardiner Houlgate.

Teacher 'abused trust' by having sex with pupil

Urgent repairs for 'dangerous' entry at abbey

Dry summer puts horse racing season under threat

Standout items from the sale included a photograph of Du Pre playing her first cello as a child, which sold for £1,100, her birth certificate that went for £1,000, and a collection of tunes composed by her mother, which sold for £4,000.

Du Pre's childhood teddy, Sebastian, also sold for £620.

South said the "incredibly personal" nature of the items might have attracted the buyers.

Jaquelin Du Pre performed her first cello concert at the age of seven and went on to become one of the most renowned instrumentalists of the 20th Century before her death in 1987 at the age of 42.

The sale was organised by Du Pre's sister, Hilary Finzi, who previously said many of the items had been "stored in our homes for decades".

South said Finzi "not only attended the auction but made a presentation at the start".

This is the first auction of du Pre's belongings, with a second one planned for December.

"We've tried to arrange it so it's chronological, this was very much about the first part of her career and her childhood," said South.

"The second part of the sale in December will be more about her glittering career and obviously her sad death."

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial live updates: Mistrial declared after last-minute defense appeal is denied
articles.summary: The judge said he would declare a mistrial Friday after the jury weighing the fate of Lindsay Clancy failed for the third time to reach a verdict in the case. Clancy's lawyer stepped in and said he wanted to appeal to a higher court. The judge granted him one hour to do so.
articles.body:
What to know about the trial The judge declared a mistrial today after the jury weighing the fate of Lindsay Clancy failed for the third time to reach a verdict in the case. The jury told Judge William Sullivan it was hopelessly deadlocked in the murder trial of Clancy, who killed her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — at their home in Massachusetts before she tried to kill herself in January 2023. Clancy's lawyer stepped in at the last minute and said he wanted to appeal to a higher court. The judge granted him one hour to do so, but the top court in Massachusetts declined the appeal. Jurors were deliberating over charges of first-degree murder — involving “deliberate premeditation and extreme atrocity” — with the option to consider lesser manslaughter charges. Clancy’s mental health is a key issue. Her defense, led by attorney Kevin Reddington, argued she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and was compelled to act by a hallucinated voice when she strangled her children. Since she suffered from a mental disease, the defense argued, she's not criminally responsible. The prosecution’s closing argument, delivered by Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague, said Clancy was a “functioning mom” who knew “right and wrong.” Clancy put a level of planning into the killings that indicates she wasn't psychotic, Sprague argued. The nearly six-week trial has taken over podcasts, social media and conversations beyond the Massachusetts courtroom. Clancy, 36, has also emerged as a symbol of the gaps in maternal healthcare.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy lawyer Kevin Reddington creates courtroom spectacles
articles.summary: Kevin Reddington has transfixed audiences defending the US mother accused of killing her children.
articles.body:
From gentle protector to throwing papers in frustration at the murder trial of US mother Lindsay Clancy, defence lawyer Kevin Reddington has been a captivating presence during the proceedings.

He's held her hand, rubbed her shoulder, gently escorted her across the courtroom in her wheelchair.

He's stood before the jury, arguing with calm conviction that Clancy, 36, was a mother in need of help, not a calculated killer who coldly murdered her three children.

Reddington has softly referred to "this young lady" and with his voice elevated during closing arguments, declared: "This is a prosecution that has ripped the soul out of this girl".

A spectacle for the global audiences captivated by proceedings broadcast from the courtroom, such dramatics are nothing new for those who have followed Reddington's career.

Reddington first made national headlines in 1989, when he won freedom for Therese Rogers, a woman accused of killing her boyfriend after stabbing his eyes out, the Cape Cod Times reported. (She did so with a butcher's knife, the court would learn, while the boyfriend slept.)

During the case, Reddington threw a pair of ninja stars across the courtroom to demonstrate their lethality. The scars in the wall remained decades later.

He had employed an insanity defence, the Times noted, telling the jury Rogers had suffered years of abuse from her boyfriend and developed Battered Woman Syndrome that resulted in a temporary bout of insanity when she killed him.

His successful use of that insanity argument was the first of its kind, according to the New York Times.

He relied on a similar argument in another case in 2007, when another woman was accused of killing her husband with a single gunshot to the chest, according to local news outlet The Enterprise.

Reddington presented such strong evidence that the woman had been abused that a grand jury failed to even return an indictment against her. In the US, such panels are convened by prosecutors to hear evidence to determine if there is enough to warrant criminal charges.

Follow live - all the latest updates and analysis

What happens next after Lindsay Clancy's murder case ended in a mistrial?

It was an incredible feat, Boston-based lawyer Rosemary Scapicchio told The Enterprise. She cited a humorous adage among the US legal community - that the bar for evidence is so low for grand juries to issue indictments, they would indict "a ham sandwich".

Reddington's fame peaked again around 2011, when defending Catherine Greig, the girlfriend of notorious mob boss James Whitey Bulger - played by Johnny Depp in the movie Black Mass.

She got a plea deal after harbouring one of the FBI's then-Ten Most Wanted fugitives for years.

Now, with the world watching to find out the fate of Clancy, all eyes are on Reddington once again.

On Friday, the court saw his emotions flare amid a heated discussion with the judge, as he pleaded with the judge not to declare a mistrial.

A day earlier, he had raised his voice, slammed a stack of papers, then sat visibly agitated, adjusting his coffee mug after the judge declined to remove a juror at Reddington's request.

Reddington had appeared to be on the verge of another high-profile acquittal and said the lone holdout was not applying the law correctly, preventing a unanimous verdict as required.

On Friday, he persuaded the judge to grant a one-hour delay before declaring a mistrial, which would require retrying the whole case.

"If we come back here in a half an hour with a mistrial because of a juror that has just spurned the instructions of this court", Reddington said, "it's a shame. It's a real shame".

The judge initially declined, at one point saying "I'm not an actor", but then acceded to Reddington's request, allowing him to appeal to the highest court in Massachusetts.

When the judge did declare a mistrial, a date was set for Reddington to argue again for a not guilty finding instead.

articles.title: Witkoff, Kushner to visit Russia, Ukraine in effort to jump-start peace talks
articles.summary: Two top U.S. envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, will travel to Russia and Ukraine this weekend in an effort to restart peace negotiations between the two countries, according to multiple reports. Witkoff and Kushner — President Trump’s special envoy and son-in-law, respectively — will first meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on…
articles.body:
Two top U.S. envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, will travel to Russia and Ukraine this weekend in an effort to restart peace negotiations between the two countries, according to multiple reports.

Witkoff and Kushner — President Trump’s special envoy and son-in-law, respectively — will first meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, The New York Times reported.

The duo will then travel to Kyiv on Sunday to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, a Ukrainian source with knowledge of these plans confirmed to The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation.

Zelensky also confirmed the U.S. delegation’s trip to Kyiv in a statement shared on social media Friday afternoon, citing details confirmed by Trump’s team.

The Ukrainian leader confirmed his military will hold off on launching airstrikes during this trip “so that the negotiators can arrive safely.”

“Our goal is to make the visit and the talks with the U.S. side as constructive and substantive as possible,” Zelensky wrote. “We need to look for real options for how to move this war toward an end. We will see what proposals Steve and Jared bring and what they are told in Moscow in response.”

The details of these peace talks have not been disclosed. The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

The trip will mark the first trip to the Ukrainian capital for both Witkoff and Kushner. Both men have made several visits to Moscow during the conflict. It also follows CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s unannounced visit to Moscow last week.

Russian state-run news agency TASS reported Friday that the U.S. envoys planned to travel to the country “soon,” citing unnamed sources.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in a Friday statement shared by TASS that there are no set conditions yet to reach a peace agreement with Ukraine.

“Unfortunately, there are no specific prerequisites yet. Work continues and communication is ongoing,” Peskov added, according to the state-run outlet.

The reported travel plans come amid escalating attacks in the years-long war between Russia and Ukraine, as each side rejects the other’s demands and Putin continues to push Ukraine to give up a large portion of its territory.

Moscow has launched a near-continuous attack on Kyiv for the past eight days, striking buildings, warehouses and the central headquarters for Ukraine’s security service. Ukraine’s military has responded with long-range attacks on Russian oil storage and refining facilities.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Arnold Schwarzenegger: "Never follow the crowd, go where it's…" - a powerful advice on success
articles.summary: US News: Arnold Schwarzenegger's quote is a genuinely powerful reminder about individuality, courage and finding real opportunity precisely where other people .
articles.body: Arnold Schwarzenegger's quote is a genuinely powerful reminder about individuality, courage and finding real opportunity precisely where other people are not already looking. "Never follow the crowd, go where it's empty," he wrote in his 2012 memoir, Total Recall: My Unbelievably True Life Story, a line found on page 766 of the book. The fuller original passage carries even more weight than the short version usually shared online. "Don't go where it's crowded," he actually continued. "Go where it's empty. Even though it's harder to get there, that's where you belong and where there's less competition." The idea was never that following others is always genuinely wrong. Sometimes the conventional path is genuinely sensible. When everyone is competing for exactly the same opportunity, though, standing apart can genuinely make it easier to create something distinctive, and Schwarzenegger's own life offers a genuinely useful example of exactly what that actually looks like in practice.Quote of the day by Arnold Schwarzenegger"Never follow the crowd, go where it's empty"What is the meaning of Arnold Schwarzenegger's quoteSchwarzenegger is encouraging people to look genuinely beyond whatever everyone else happens to be doing. When a particular career or business idea becomes popular, more people naturally move toward it, and competition genuinely increases as a result, making it considerably harder to actually stand out. An "empty" path represents an area where genuinely fewer people are actively competing. Finding that path requires real curiosity and a genuine willingness to make decisions based on your own judgement, rather than simply copying whatever the crowd happens to already be doing.Why following the crowd can genuinely feel easierPeople naturally look to others when making a real decision. If many people are choosing the exact same career or pursuing the exact same goal, it can genuinely create the impression that the choice must be correct simply because so many people made it. There is real comfort in being part of a larger group. Popularity, though, does not necessarily mean something is genuinely the best fit for you specifically. A crowded path may simply be crowded because everyone else is following everyone else in turn.Why taking a genuinely different path can create real opportunityWhen genuinely fewer people are pursuing something, there tends to be considerably less competition. That can create real opportunity for someone willing to develop a different skill, explore an overlooked market, or approach a genuinely familiar problem in a new way. Being different never automatically leads to success on its own, but it can make your own work considerably easier for other people to actually notice and distinguish from everyone else's.Schwarzenegger's own career genuinely reflects this ideaSchwarzenegger built his career across several genuinely different fields entirely. He became a successful bodybuilder before establishing himself as a Hollywood actor, and later entered politics, serving as Governor of California. Each real transition required him to enter a genuinely new environment and build fresh credibility almost from scratch. His career genuinely demonstrates the value of having the confidence to pursue an opportunity that may not initially look like the obvious route to anyone watching from outside.Being genuinely different does not mean being recklessThe quote should never be read as an instruction to reject every popular idea outright. A genuinely crowded field can still contain excellent opportunity. The real lesson here is simply to think carefully before actually following. Ask honestly why everyone is genuinely moving in the same direction. Consider whether the opportunity genuinely suits you personally, and then examine whether another route might actually produce a considerably better result. Taking a different path should genuinely involve real judgement, not simply a desire to seem different for its own sake.Why genuinely independent thinking mattersIndependent thinking lets people genuinely question their own assumptions. Instead of asking what everyone else is doing, you can genuinely ask what actually makes sense for you specifically. That small shift can reveal real possibilities that might otherwise stay completely overlooked, and it can also encourage genuine creativity, since you are no longer limiting yourself purely to an already established pattern.The genuine fear of going somewhere "empty"An empty path can genuinely feel intimidating too. If nobody else is doing something, there may be genuinely less certainty about what will actually happen next. There may be no established roadmap, fewer real examples to actually follow, and a genuinely greater possibility of failure along the way. That real uncertainty is precisely why courage actually matters here. Sometimes an empty path is empty because it genuinely has no potential at all. Sometimes, though, it is simply empty because too few people have actually been willing to explore it properly.Other memorable quotes by Arnold Schwarzenegger"Be hungry for success, hungry to make your mark, hungry to be seen and to be heard and to have an effect. And as you move up and become successful, make sure also to be hungry for helping others.""To be successful, however, you must be brutal with yourself and focus on the flaws.""Strength does not come from winning. Your struggles develop your strengths. When you go through hardships and decide not to surrender, that is strength.""It's easier to stand out when you aim straight for the top."How to apply Arnold Schwarzenegger's lessonQuestion a genuinely popular choice, since popularity never automatically makes something right for you specifically. Look genuinely for an overlooked opportunity, paying real attention to areas receiving considerably less attention than everyone else's focus. Develop your own genuine strengths, since your unique ability may actually work better pursued in an unconventional direction entirely. Do genuine research too, since a less crowded path should still carry real potential underneath it, and take a calculated risk rather than a reckless one, since different was never meant to simply mean careless. Avoid copying blindly, learning from other people without simply replicating their own choices, and try to think genuinely long term, considering where a path could actually lead rather than only what happens to be popular today.Why Arnold Schwarzenegger's quote remains relevantModern life can genuinely make following the crowd feel almost effortless. Trends spread quickly, popular careers attract thousands of people at once, and social media constantly shows everyone exactly what everyone else is already doing. Schwarzenegger's words offer a genuine reason to pause before joining that rush automatically. The most obvious path is not necessarily the genuinely most rewarding one available. Sometimes the greatest real opportunity actually lies somewhere considerably fewer people are willing to go looking for it. Finding that opportunity requires considerably more than simply avoiding the crowd for its own sake. It requires real curiosity, genuine preparation, and the confidence to actually trust your own judgement, even when everyone else around you clearly appears to be heading in a completely different direction.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Serbia accused of ‘glorifying’ convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić ahead of funeral
articles.summary: BELGRADE, Serbia — The European Union’s Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Friday canceled an upcoming visit to candidate nation Serbia over what she described as the “glorification” of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladić following his death.
articles.body: BELGRADE, Serbia — The European Union’s Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Friday canceled an upcoming visit to candidate nation Serbia over what she described as the “glorification” of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladić following his death. Mladić was convicted of genocide by a U.N. court but remains a hero to many Serbs. Mladić’s remains were flown to Belgrade on a Serbian government plane from The Hague, Netherlands, on Thursday, a week after his death and days ahead of his burial in a Belgrade cemetery. Mladić was sentenced in 2017 to life imprisonment for orchestrating the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslims in Srebrenica in 1995; the yearslong siege of the Bosnian capital of Sarajevo during the 1992-95 conflict; and other war crimes, including setting up concentration camps for detained non-Serb civilians and enemy soldiers. Upon landing in Belgrade, Mladić’s coffin was wrapped in the national flag and Serbian soldiers carried his body to a van for transport to the military hospital. Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic was on the plane with Mladić’s family members and nationalist admirers lit flares as the convoy passed. Kos said on X that “the glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.” “Ratko Mladić was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes,” Kos said. “The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history.” In Belgrade, regional N1 television quoted Serbia’s populist President Aleksandar Vučić as saying that Kos’s explanation was “very short but stupid.” Vučić said Kos did not specify “who glorified anything” but that “I guess we should ban people from showing up, ban the funeral.” Earlier Friday, Kos said the next days “will be a very important test” for Serbia ahead of the burial, which could draw thousands of admirers. Mladić to be buried Monday in Belgrade Mladić’s son, Darko Mladić, said at a news conference Friday that a military commemoration is planned for Saturday. Mladić’s coffin will be placed in a church in Belgrade on Monday morning so people can pay their respects before his funeral and burial later that day. Vučić had previously said Mladić would be buried with full state honors, sparking outrage across the Balkans, where ethnic divisions persist decades after the 1992-95 war in Bosnia killed over 100,000 people and displaced millions. Last year, Serbia buried another convicted war criminal, the former army chief of staff Nebojša Pavković, with full military honors at a cemetery for distinguished individuals. Serbia, which backed Bosnian Serb forces during the war, is formally seeking EU membership but remains defiant over its war role, accusing the West of anti-Serb bias. After Mladić died last week, thousands of Serbs in their political entity in Bosnia and many in Serbia held vigils in his honor. Thousands could attend the funeral. Other European officials condemn Mladić glorification The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O’Flaherty, on Friday urged authorities in Serbia and in the Serb-run entity of Bosnia to “counter the glorification of convicted war criminals,” which is illegal in Bosnia and “is not protected speech under the European Convention on Human Rights.” “I abhor the public glorification of Ratko Mladić, a deceased war criminal convicted for the Srebrenica genocide and crimes against humanity,” O’Flaherty said in a statement. Belgium’s Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said granting funeral honors for Mladić would be “shameful and disrespectful for the victims,” adding: “I condemn that act in the strongest terms, and have passed this message to my Serbian counterpart in charge of European affairs this morning.” Calls are also multiplying for Europe’s biggest political bloc - the European People’s Party - to cut its ties to Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is a member of the EPP, along with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and other top officials. Vladimir Prebilic, a European Parliament member from Slovenia, urged the EPP to “stop acting as a safe haven” for Vučić’s party, which he said “openly celebrates convicted war criminals and rolls out the red carpet for the ‘Butcher of Bosnia.”’ Serbia’s president says he has meetings on Monday In Serbia, Vučić, who is a former extreme nationalist who backed Serbia’s expansionist policies in the past, said Friday that he has previously scheduled meetings Monday, and the funeral arrangements were made by Mladić’s family. “I have spoken to the Mladić family and I wish it all passes in a dignified way,” Vučić said, according to the pro-government Informer television. “I did all I could so that the funeral would pass as it should,” he added without elaborating. Serbia’s EU bid has stalled due to democratic backsliding and Vučić’s refusal to join international sanctions against Russia over the invasion of Ukraine. The massacre in Srebrenica was Europe’s first acknowledged genocide after World War II. A U.N. “safe haven” for Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims), Srebrenica ended up being overrun by Serbs who forced men and boys to strip, killed them and bulldozed their bodies into mass graves. Mladić was one of the most notorious figures of the war in Bosnia that left more than 100,000 people dead and over 1 million homeless before it ended in 1995 in a U.S.-brokered peace agreement.

articles.title: Villagers vow to rebuild despite devastating mass demolition in West Bank
articles.summary: Israeli forces’ demolition of 12 homes in Khirbet al-Tabban leaves villagers determined to stand firm on their land.
articles.body:
Khirbet al-Tabban, occupied West Bank – The signs of the mass demolition were visible everywhere in Khirbet al-Tabban: destroyed homes, scattered rubble, empty animal pens, and water tanks and essential facilities that were no longer there.

A woman sits beneath a tractor trailer, trying to shelter from the heat of the sun. Beside her are some of the belongings she had managed to save from the demolition.

On Wednesday, Israeli forces arrived unannounced in this small village in the southern West Bank’s Masafer Yatta region, and demolished all of its 12 homes, as well as most of the community’s other structures, leaving about 70 people homeless.

Nidal Younis, head of the Masafer Yatta Council, describes the demolition as “wiping the village off the face of the earth”. But he’s insistent that the villagers will not leave, despite repeated attempts by Israel to force Palestinians out across Masafer Yatta.

“The decision to remain and stand firm is the people’s own decision,” Younis says. “They see no alternative to this land.”

But in Khirbet al-Tabban, remaining means sleeping in the open.

With water sources and sanitation facilities destroyed, Younis says the residents’ immediate priorities are shelter, drinking water and sanitation facilities.

He warns that tents will not be sufficient against the strong winds and cold that will arrive in the next few months, especially for children, women, older people and the sick.

And he’s fearful that what happened in Khirbet al-Tabban is likely to be repeated in other Masafer Yatta villages, following a 2022 Israeli court decision to allow for the displacement of the residents from the area after Israel designated it a military firing zone decades earlier.

Israel justified Wednesday’s demolition by saying the buildings were unauthorised. It is almost impossible for Palestinians in Area C of the occupied West Bank – which Masafer Yatta lies in – to get authorisation, even outside of military firing zones. Demolitions have become regular occurrences.

“The goal, as we see it, is to displace Palestinians and change the reality of these areas,” Younis says.

Nasser Mahmoud Obeid, one of the Khirbet al-Tabban villagers, says that Israeli forces ordered the residents to “get out by force” when they arrived on Wednesday morning.

The order wasn’t entirely unfamiliar to Obeid – he remembers a major demolition that took place in 1999, and has had to endure years of attacks from the Israeli army and settlers since then.

Obeid set to work after the Israelis left this week to clear the rubble and prepare temporary places to sleep.

He insists to Al Jazeera that the villagers will ultimately rebuild everything. Obeid says he was born in Khirbet al-Tabban in 1977, and that his father and grandfather lived there before him.

“This is our land, and here we will build and rebuild,” he says. “You can see with your own eyes what we are doing. We have not lost hope, and we will not.”

Suad Mohammed Obeid, 48, stood among the remains of the place where she had lived for more than three decades.

She searched through the rubble for her belongings, stopping at objects that had been part of her daily life, including the sewing machine she used to make clothes for her husband, who works in a metalworking shop, as well as for her children and grandchildren.

Suad has lived in Khirbet al-Tabban for 32 years, moving to the village after she got married. Over the years, her life became closely tied to agriculture, livestock and the production of dairy products, including cheese and yoghurt.

“They demolished all of Khirbet al-Tabban and wiped it off the face of the earth,” she says.

“The night after the demolition was very difficult for us, our children, and our grandchildren,” she says. “The children are not used to sleeping outside their rooms, and we are already afraid to sleep outdoors because of settler attacks.”

She says the children remained frightened and awake throughout the night.

“Today we are out in the open. There is nowhere for us to shelter.”

She believes that what happened is part of an attempt by Israel to make life impossible for Palestinians in the West Bank, through demolitions, preventing access to grazing land, and attacks by settlers.

But she insists: “God willing, organisations will help us and provide us with tents, and we will remain steadfast.”

articles.title: Chinese man studying in Canada arrested by US for espionage-like activities, sister says 'If my brother is a Chinese spy, then I am Trump's father'
articles.summary: US News: A Chinese student studying at a Canadian university has been arrested in the United States after US authorities accused him of taking photographs at a.
articles.body: A Chinese student studying at a Canadian university has been arrested in the United States after US authorities accused him of taking photographs at airports and freight facilities at the request of a person he allegedly believed was connected to the Chinese government.Weiheng Zeng, an undergraduate student at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, was arrested in Michigan on August 23 after crossing the Ambassador Bridge between Canada and the US.Zeng has been charged with making false statements to federal authorities. He has not been charged with espionage, and the allegations contained in an FBI affidavit have not been tested in court.The case began with an incident at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport in April.According to an affidavit filed in a Michigan court, a man was seen taking photographs at a FedEx cargo facility on April 21. The man allegedly climbed onto a forklift and attempted to open locked trailers.Investigators later linked the incident to a dark blue minivan with Ontario licence plates. About four months later, on August 23, Zeng attempted to enter the US again in the same vehicle. He was pulled aside by border officers and questioned before FBI agents became involved.What followed were three interviews in which, according to the affidavit, Zeng gave investigators increasingly detailed and conflicting accounts of what he had been doing.Initially, Zeng said he had travelled to Chicago to photograph aircraft. He had told US customs officers that he was visiting his sister.Severeal photos of aircraft, military planes on phoneAgents searching his phone allegedly found photographs of aircraft, including military planes. They also found photographs of Zeng and other people wearing tactical clothing and holding rifle-style firearms.Zeng told investigators the weapons were airsoft guns and said he had been photographing aircraft models for a flight-tracking website. He also denied having military training.During a later interview, he reportedly said he had photographed planes landing at O'Hare from a public parking lot. He subsequently acknowledged going to the FedEx facility and climbing onto a forklift to take photographs.The affidavit also alleged that Zeng had previously trespassed at a FedEx facility at Toronto Pearson International Airport in Canada, where he was caught.But investigators say the most significant details emerged during a third interview.Chinese contact approached through a website for aviation enthusiastsZeng allegedly told them that a Chinese contact had approached him through a website used by aviation enthusiasts and asked him to photograph specific aircraft. The contact supplied aircraft tail numbers and allegedly paid him between $20 and $30 for each photograph.According to the affidavit, the contact also sent Zeng SIM cards to use for communications. Zeng said he would destroy the cards and delete conversations and photographs after completing assignments.He told investigators that he had accepted assignments at O'Hare and Pearson, but rejected requests to photograph locations in Orlando and Las Vegas.The Chinese contact initially presented the assignments as aviation “research”, with Zeng allegedly told to photograph rare aircraft.But investigators say Zeng eventually acknowledged that the aircraft explanation was a cover.The contact was allegedly interested instead in transportation logistics and photographs of specific locations around airports.Zeng also allegedly told the FBI that the contact had sent him a photograph of a badge and videos showing scenes that appeared accessible only to security officials.According to the affidavit, Zeng had been communicating with the contact for about three months beginning in late 2024. He said the person eventually asked him for “help”, and he agreed because he thought it was “cool.”The alleged payments were made through transfers to a Bank of China account, the affidavit says. Investigators also discovered that the online forum where Zeng said he had met the contact apparently did not exist.'If my brother is a Chinese spy, then I'm Trump's father'Zeng's sister denied the allegations that her brother is knowingly involved in espionage for Beijing. "If my brother is a Chinese spy, then I'm Trump's father," Meixuan Wang wrote in a social media post on Wednesday.Wang told the Globe and Mail that her brother is just obsessed with airplanes and has autism spectrum disorder.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Brazilian Supreme Court roiled by dispute between justices
articles.summary: The country’s highest court is considering investigations into two judges who have accused each other of wrongdoing.
articles.body:
Brazil’s Supreme Court has found itself at the centre of a corruption scandal roiling the country, with the body considering investigations into two justices who have accused each other of wrongdoing.

The dispute centres on Justice Alexandre de Moraes , who oversaw the case that convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro, and Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee.

Mendonca released a report this week showing alleged links between de Moraes and disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro, accused of a wide-reaching fraud scheme.

De Moraes subsequently accused Mendonca of abusing his authority by unsealing the documents.

Chief Justice Edson Fachin said on Friday that he would give Brazil’s attorney general five days to weigh the allegations against Mendonca.

The court is also set to decide next week whether to investigate de Moraes.

“This may be the most dramatic moment in the history of Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court,” said Felipe Recondo, a journalist and researcher who is a longtime observer of the court.

The right has pounced on the allegations against de Moraes to cast doubt on the case against Bolsonaro, who is currently under house arrest after receiving a 27-year prison sentence for his involvement in a coup plot.

Following his loss to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in 2022, prosecutors say Bolsonaro and his far-right allies sought to subvert the election results and derail the transition of power.

Post-election tensions culminated in an attack on key government buildings in the capital Brasilia on January 8, 2023, led by Bolsonaro supporters who allegedly hoped to trigger a military uprising.

In November 2024, Brazil’s federal police recommended charges be brought against Bolsonaro and a group of his key allies.

Bolsonaro, however, has portrayed the case as a “witch hunt” orchestrated by the left. He has received support from high-profile figures, including United States President Donald Trump.

De Moraes oversaw the Bolsonaro case, putting him at the centre of a political firestorm.

Trump’s Treasury Department briefly sanctioned De Moraes for his involvement in the Bolsonaro trial, as well as his suspensions of online platforms like Rumble and X, the latter run by Trump ally Elon Musk.

De Moraes was appointed to the Supreme Court under the presidency of Michel Temer, a centre-right politician, and he has since become a target for Brazil’s far-right, due to his involvement in sensitive cases, including Bolsonaro’s.

Experts like Recondo say the Supreme Court has served as a intermediary in some of Brazil’s most heated political fights.

“The Supreme Court can provide some balance in that game,” said Recondo. “Remove the court from that position, and all that remains is conflict. And that is a problem.”

The Vorcaro fraud scandal, however, threatens to tarnish the court’s reputation. This week’s unsealed documents suggest that the banker Vorcaro may have reached out to de Moraes for advice.

Politicians have called for de Moraes to clarify his relationship with the disgraced banker, with some calling for his resignation.

Candidates on both the right and left have both sought to portray each other as corrupt in the run-up to the country’s contentious presidential election on October 4.

That race will see the left-wing Lula face off against Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.

The right-wing candidate has sought to capitalise on the scandal, painting it as a conspiracy between de Moraes and the political left to dismantle his father’s legacy.

“Out with Lula! Out with Moraes! This duo has no place left in leading the Country,” Senator Bolsonaro said in a recent social media post. “It’s time for change! Brazil will win!”

The younger Bolsonaro, however, has also been tarnished by his connections to Vorcaro.

Earlier this year, the US investigative news website The Intercept Brasil published messages reportedly between Flavio Bolsonaro and Vorcaro, whom the senator was petitioning for funding.

The funding was slated to go to a film about his father, Jair Bolsonaro. Vorcaro reportedly pledged millions of dollars to back the film project. Senator Bolsonaro has denied any wrongdoing, calling it a private project.

articles.title: Five EU nations inch towards deal on migrant ‘return hubs’ by 2027
articles.summary: Germany, Austria, ⁠Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands did not outline where the centres would be located.
articles.body:
Five European nations have agreed on concrete steps towards a deal with an unspecified non-European Union country to host migrant return facilities, senior officials said, in a sign of mounting determination to counter immigration.

Germany, Austria, ⁠Greece, Denmark and the Netherlands, known as the Group of Five, aim to sign deals this year to send migrants without legal residency to countries outside the European Union. The nations expected to host return centres have not been named.

“Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union,” Danish Immigration and Integration Minister Morten Bodskov told reporters on Friday at a news conference in Copenhagen, without elaborating.

“It’s a new chance to have a life in a partner country,” he said, adding ‌that the five nations would be in dialogue with the International Organization for Migration and the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) on their next steps.

A spokesperson for UNHCR said the agency had not been approached with ‌details ‌of the proposal and therefore could not comment.

The Group of Five is set to reconvene in Munich, Germany, at the end of September to advance the plan.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt confirmed that the group wants “to reach an agreement with ‌third countries this year that will enable the establishment of return hubs”.

The European Parliament in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to set up centres abroad, in what some critics of the policy say could weaken safeguards for asylum seekers.

The Council of ⁠Europe, a non-EU body that promotes human rights, democracy and the rule of ⁠law, said in July that the proposed return hubs posed “considerable human rights risks”.

Danish Refugee Council Secretary-General Charlotte Slente said a better policy would be to implement the EU Pact on Migration and Asylum, which focuses ⁠on stricter border screening, faster return procedures and expanded digital systems for managing asylum claims.

“Return hubs focus on a small number of returns; they ⁠will not stop people from taking even more dangerous routes, and ⁠they could violate basic human rights,” she said.

articles.title: Joseph Martinek bought a Texas farm in 1911; 115 years later, his descendants donated a conservation easement protecting 470 acres of farmland, wildlife habitat and open space
articles.summary: US News: Martinek Farm, located outside La Grange in Fayette County, Texas, has become the county’s latest conservation success story. The property, which has .
articles.body: Martinek Farm, located outside La Grange in Fayette County, Texas, has become the county’s latest conservation success story. The property, which has remained connected to the same family since 1911, is now permanently protected through a donated conservation easement.The easement was contributed by longtime landowners Russell and Debbie Friemel and Ardie Friemel Holsinger in honour of their great-grandfather, Joseph Martinek, whose purchase of the property more than 100 years ago began the family’s relationship with the land.A family legacy dating back to 1911According to Texas Land Conservancy, Joseph Martinek purchased the property in 1911, establishing a tradition of farming and caring for the land that continued through generations.In the 1980s, siblings Russell Friemel and Ardie Friemel Holsinger inherited the family property. They continued its working-land legacy while maintaining the connection to their great-grandfather’s original purchase.The family began exploring permanent conservation of the property in 2021. Five years later, in 2026, the process culminated in the donation of a conservation easement.A conservation easement is a voluntary legal agreement that permanently limits certain future uses of a property in order to protect its conservation values. Importantly, the family retains ownership of Martinek Farm and can continue managing it as working land.Protecting a vulnerable part of the Colorado River basinThe 470-acre property sits in a vulnerable part of the Colorado River basin, where surrounding development and industrial activities pose growing challenges to natural habitats, scenic open spaces and water resources.Surface mining, highway-related development and oil and gas extraction are among the land uses occurring in the wider region.By placing the property under permanent conservation protection, the family has helped preserve a significant stretch of undeveloped landscape while creating a long-term safeguard for its natural resources.Ross Creek adds to the property's ecological importanceOne of the farm’s most important natural features is Ross Creek, a spring-fed waterway that contributes water throughout the year to an ecologically significant section of the Colorado River.The undeveloped land surrounding the creek plays an important role in maintaining the health of its riparian ecosystem. Vegetation and open land can help filter rainfall, reduce erosion and protect water quality while providing habitat for wildlife.The wider river system is home to several threatened or endangered aquatic species, including the blue sucker, Tampico pearly mussel, pimpleback mussel and Texas fawnsfoot mussel.Martinek Farm itself supports a variety of aquatic species, including bass, cichlid and sunfish.Farmland and wildlife habitat protected togetherThe conservation value of Martinek Farm extends beyond its waterways. Nearly half of the property’s soils meet the criteria for Farmland of Statewide Importance, making the land valuable for producing food, feed, forage and fibre.The agricultural landscape also provides a range of habitats for native species.Open oak savannah and prairie grasslands dotted with live oaks dominate parts of the uplands, while denser oak-yaupon woodlands provide cover for woodland wildlife. Along Ross Creek and its floodplains, bottomland and riparian forests create a shaded corridor connecting different upland and wetland habitats.Freshwater ponds, wetlands and other open-water areas further add to the ecological diversity of the property.A landscape with deep Texas historyMartinek Farm is also significant because of its historical and archaeological resources. The property contains archaeological evidence associated with periods ranging from the Late Paleoindian to Late Archaic periods, as well as the era of colonial settlement in Texas.The area's history is also linked to James J. Ross, an early Texas settler and member of Stephen F. Austin’s “Old Three Hundred.”A Texas Historical Marker erected nearby in 1985 notes Ross's role as a farmer, rancher, trader and merchant and describes his influence on the early settlement of the region. Ross Prairie and Ross Creek were named after him.The marker also records that Ross’s home eventually became known as the Ross/Martinek House, which was owned by Czech immigrant Joseph Martinek and his descendants for nearly seven decades.The property’s archaeological importance received further recognition in 2025, when the Texas Historical Commission designated a State Archeological Landmark at Martinek Farm.Conservation protects more than landFor the Friemel family, the conservation easement represents more than the preservation of acreage. It ensures that a property tied to their family for generations will continue to provide agricultural, ecological and historical value long into the future.The process began with conversations among family members and a land trust and involved expert advice, service providers and support from a grant through the Texas Land Trust Council.Texas Land Conservancy also acknowledged the contribution of Russell, Debbie and Ardie, describing the conservation easement as a significant gift to Texas’s natural resources, history and future generations.More than a century after Joseph Martinek purchased the land, his descendants have ensured that the 470-acre property will remain protected while the family continues to own and steward it, turning a 1911 land purchase into a conservation legacy for generations yet to come.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: UN votes to adopt new world map that reflects Africa’s true size
articles.summary: The widely-used Mercator map is often criticised for visually exaggerating and centralising Western nations.
articles.body:
The United Nations has voted to adopt a new world map that more accurately reflects countries’ true sizes, a resolution sponsored by African states to right a centuries-old wrong.

The “Correct the Map” resolution adopted by the UN general assembly on Friday aims to address a colonial-era injustice that has visually shrunk Africa for 450 years, shaping how the continent is perceived in media, education and policy around the world.

The resolution, put forward by African Union (AU) member states and the Bahamas, was backed by a vote of 164-1 with six abstentions.

Togo led the AU’s campaign to limit use of the widely-used Mercator map.

Developed in the 16th century by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator, the projection distorts the relative size of land masses by expanding those nearer the poles. For instance, it makes Greenland appear roughly the same size as Africa, even though Africa is about 14 times larger.

Some critics of the Mercator map believe it remains widely used because it visually exaggerates and centralises Western nations, perpetuating ideas of European superiority.

“A fair world begins with a fair map,” Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey told the Reuters news agency ahead of Friday’s vote.

The resolution promotes the Equal Earth projection, which more accurately portrays the size of the continents.

The resolution is not legally binding and it “in no way challenges the use of the Mercator projection for maritime and aerial navigation, for which it remains fully suited,” the Togolese ministry said in a statement.

The United States – the only country to vote against the resolution – said it promoted an “ideological agenda” and was a distraction from the “genuine problems of international peace, prosperity or good relations”.

Moky Makura, executive director of the advocacy organisation Africa No Filter that’s involved in “Correct the World” map campaign, hailed the vote, saying “now the real work begins”.

“We want to see accurate maps in schools, textbooks, newsrooms, businesses and on the digital platforms billions of people use every day,” Makura said in a statement.

“If we got something as basic as Africa’s size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning? Africa doesn’t need to be made bigger. It needs to be seen accurately,” she added.

‘Distortions eventually take root in perceptions’

Ahead of the vote, France, who co-sponsored the resolution, announced that it planned to abandon the Mercator map.

The foreign ministry “will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris.

“The United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia,” Barrot said, adding that “distortions eventually take root in perceptions” and that “the time has come to correct them.”

The Mercator map remains widely used in classrooms, but Togo hopes to change its school geography materials by the end of the year, Dussey told Reuters.

Togo will press other governments, schools, international organisations and technology companies to move away from the Mercator map in favour of the Equal Earth one, Dussey said.

Dussey linked the campaign to adopt the map to wider African efforts to confront colonial-era legacies, while saying it was not an attack on Europe or any other civilisation.

The Mercator map’s widespread use is a consequence of colonisation, he said.

“The world is changing. Africa also is changing.”

articles.title: PMLA court: Cheques, drugs constitute proceeds of crime
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Broadening the definition of \"property\" under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, a special PMLA court in Mohali has ruled that seized bank.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Broadening the definition of "property" under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, a special PMLA court in Mohali has ruled that seized bank cheques, even if not encashed, and narcotics both fall under the definition of "property" and constitute proceeds of crime under the money laundering Act.The judgement came Thursday, when ED launched a massive search operation at 30 premises across all zones of the southern region in different narcotics-related cases. The searches are being conducted under the mandate of Centre's 'Nasha Mukt Bharat' campaign with targets in the first phase spread across Kerala, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Telangana.The judge convicted two accused and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for three years, while rejecting the contention of the defence that their property and bank accounts were not attached and the seized contraband could not be considered proceeds of crime as no money trail had been brought on the record.Special judge Hardip Singh also rejected the defence's argument that the cheques recovered from the accused were not encashed and thus could not constitute proceeds of crime. The judge noted that the cheques were exchanged for the purpose of purchasing the contraband and the accused could not provide any explanation to the contrary.Starting with the four southern states, ED Thursday began a crackdown on major drug syndicates operating across the country. The drive has been launched as part of Centre's "drug-free India" campaign to attach properties of all those engaged in drug dealing and generation of "proceeds of crime". The ED's search covered targets involved in trafficking of illicit drugs like methamphetamine, marijuana, and MDMA. Over 20 foreign nationals are under scanner, an official said.Searches were conducted at premises in Chennai, Tirunelveli, Nagapattinam, Velankanni and Ramanathapuram in Tamil Nadu; Kolar, Malur (Kolar district) and Hoskote (Bengaluru North district); Serilingampally and Nanakramguda (Hyderabad) and Ranga Reddy district in Telangana; Kozhikode, Kannur, Malappuram and Thrissur in Kerala.ED is coordinating with other central agencies and state police forces that have registered cases of drug trafficking in the past few years to further investigate the money trail and track the proceeds of crime."The investigation prima facie discloses not merely trafficking of methamphetamine, but also the generation, receipt and movement of money arising out of this," a senior official said, adding that syndicates were using hawala and crypto currency dealers to further transfer the proceeds of crime outside the country to tax havens.The money trail to uncover cash-based hawala settlements revealed "account details, transaction records, diaries, slips or tokens, mobile phones, electronic communications and digital devices, property documents and other financial records". Based on these findings, the agency ascertained the complete quantum and trail of the proceeds of crime, and the persons who received, possessed, transferred, concealed, utilised or invested such proceeds.Further these details help in identifying movable and immovable properties acquired and that leads to their attachments.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Andrew Tate indicted in Romania for trafficking minors, money laundering
articles.summary: The influencer and his brother are in a Miami prison pending potential extradition to the UK on rape charges
articles.body:
Romanian prosecutors have indicted controversial social media influencer Andrew Tate on charges of trafficking minors, sex with a minor and money laundering.

The move on Friday piles further legal pressure on Tate, who along with his brother were jailed in the United States in July after prosecutors in the United Kingdom requested their extradition on rape charges .

Romania’s anti-organised crime agency DIICOT said in a statement that Tate and his brother Tristan, who was indicted for complicity in the case, recruited their victims by falsely claiming to seek a relationship or marriage before forcing them to produce sexually exploitative content for a webcam business.

The Tate brothers have denied all wrongdoing.

DIICOT said one of Andrew Tate’s victims was 15 when he seduced her in Britain in 2012 before moving her to the Romanian capital Bucharest and using physical violence and psychological intimidation to force her into producing indecent images of children for social media.

Tristan was an accessory, the unit said, and used physical aggression to coerce the victim.

Prosecutors said the brothers kept $1.25m from the video chat income generated by the victim, or roughly 80 percent of her earnings. The brothers tried to launder the funds by buying four luxury cars, they added.

DIICOT alleges that the Tate brothers’ victims were paid or intimidated in a bid to coax them “not to give statements or to give false statements.”

Eugen Vidineac, a Romanian lawyer for the Tates, said in a statement that the brothers rejected the allegations.

“We will examine every aspect of [the indictment] with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process,” he said. “Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them.”

The Tates are former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship who amassed a vast social media following worldwide, especially among young men. Their content frequently criticised gender equality and argued for male dominance.

They were arrested in Florida in late July after the UK requested their extradition. Andrew Tate’s official social media accounts have bemoaned the conditions of his Miami jail and alleged that the charges against him are persecution for his social and political views.

Romanian authorities first opened a probe into the brothers related to potential crimes including human trafficking in December 2022, around five years after they moved to the country. Andrew Tate had boasted in online videos that he had relocated to Romania because law enforcement was more lax.

It was not immediately clear whether DIICOT would seek their extradition.

Romanian law permits the prosecution of defendants in absentia, and the case is now bound for a preliminary court chamber for a judge’s review. While the law states that the preliminary chamber judge has 60 days to finalise its advancement, indictments routinely take significantly longer.

The brothers were previously indicted in Romania on charges of human trafficking, but in late 2024 the Bucharest court of appeals sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible.

articles.title: Cambridge launches review into support for Jason Arday before death
articles.summary: The University of Cambridge says the review will look at its "decision-making and actions" before the former professor's death.
articles.body:
The University of Cambridge has launched an independent review into its "decision-making and actions" in the period leading up to former professor Jason Arday's death.

The review will examine the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.

Arday, 41, was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, the week after resigning from his position as professor of sociology of education amid intense scrutiny over allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims.

Announcing the review on Friday, Vice-Chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said the time since his death had been a "period of profound sadness and reflection for the university".

"We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus, but given the devastating outcome, we are still asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more," she said.

"This review will help us answer that question."

In a post on social media, the University of Cambridge said: "University Council took the necessary steps to launch an independent review into the university's decision-making and actions, with a focus on identifying shortcomings and areas for improvement."

The first part of the review will look at the "support, interventions and protections" available to Arday in the period before his death.

Those findings will be reported within three months, allowing recommendations for "urgent action" to be considered and implemented "without delay".

It will be led by Nazir Afzal , chancellor of the University of Manchester and former chief crown prosecutor for the North West of England.

Afzal said in a statement that "it is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity", adding "we must be willing to ask difficult questions".

The second part of the review will examine the wider circumstances of Arday's time at Cambridge, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, mentoring and support arrangements.

It will also look at the university's response to allegations of research misconduct and the support available to academics facing "extraordinary public and media scrutiny".

An independent external chair will be appointed to lead the second part of the review, with an expert panel "including individuals with lived experience" advising it.

It is expected to conclude within six months of the panel being established.

In a video message, Prentice said: "I am conscious that Professor Arday's death has deeply affected black staff and students, as well as our neurodiverse community.

"There has also been an unacceptable rise in racist, hateful, and abusive attacks on our staff and students in online forums and on social media."

In 2023, the sociologist, then 37, became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.

Arday had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. He said similar scrutiny would find comparable errors in the work of other academics.

The allegations emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said the criticism had gone "far beyond scholarly disagreement".

Resigning from his post in August , he added: "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and those I love."

Following his death, his family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

A vigil held in Trafalgar Square was attended by thousands, according to its organisers.

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage of Arday before his death.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills two in southern Lebanon amid ongoing escalation
articles.summary: Israeli attacks against villages and towns in southern Lebanon continue despite truce agreements and diplomacy.
articles.body:
An Israeli air strike targeting a motorcycle has killed two people in the Lebanese town of Kfar Reman, the Ministry of Public Health has said, as Israeli forces intensify attacks on southern Lebanon.

Lebanon’s state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported on Friday that the strike hit in Nabatieh near the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, which the Israeli army said it had captured, though Hezbollah did not confirm losing it.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz on Friday claimed the military had cleared Hezbollah fighters embedded in tunnels under the strategic ridge, which overlooks a wide area that has become one of the most hotly contested.

Israeli raids and artillery shelling also targeted seven towns in the Tyre and Nabatieh districts, causing no casualties.

NNA said the attacks hit al-Mansouri, Majdal Zoun, Buyout al-Sayyad, Beit Lif and Srebbine in the Tyre district, as well as Zawtar al-Sharqiyah and Mayfadoun in Nabatieh.

Israeli forces said they intercepted a Hezbollah drone beyond the “Yellow Line”, an area Israel has claimed as a security zone. In a statement, the military said it would strike southern Lebanon in response.

The attacks come amid continued Israeli escalation against villages and towns across southern Lebanon despite two truce agreements – on June 4 and 26 – mediated by United States President Donald Trump’s administration.

The June 4 ceasefire was contingent on a “complete cessation” of Hezbollah fire and the evacuation of its fighters from the area south of the Litani River.

The June 26 framework agreement did not specifically call for the withdrawal of the Israeli forces and instead tied it to the disarmament of Hezbollah.

Since March 2, when the latest Israeli escalation in its war on Lebanon began, Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,000 people and injured at least 12,000 others, while forcing more than one million people from their homes, according to Lebanese authorities.

Israel has expanded its military presence across swaths of southern Lebanon since launching its new campaign against Hezbollah, which fired rockets into Israel in retaliation for US-Israeli air strikes that killed Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

On Friday, Israeli authorities separately released four Lebanese people who had been held in Israeli prisons after being detained in southern Lebanon.

They were transferred to Lebanese authorities via the International Committee of the Red Cross, a day after one Lebanese man was released as part of an agreement between the two countries.

articles.title: Trump reveals Brazil, Argentina involved in controversial beef deal
articles.summary: President Trump said Friday that tariff-free imported beef will be coming from Brazil and Argentina, among other places, as his administration works to alleviate stubbornly high prices. “It’s coming from Argentina. It’s coming from Brazil,” Trump said at an Oval Office event surrounded by ranchers and farmers. “It’s coming from a couple of other places.…
articles.body:
President Trump said Friday that tariff-free imported beef will be coming from Brazil and Argentina, among other places, as his administration works to alleviate stubbornly high prices.

“It’s coming from Argentina. It’s coming from Brazil,” Trump said at an Oval Office event surrounded by ranchers and farmers. “It’s coming from a couple of other places. We have our inspectors down. It’s very clean. It’s very good.”

Trump announced last month that the U.S. would be pausing tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of beef for 90 days to be sold at a 25 percent discount below market price. The president said it would lower costs for Americans while allowing for ranchers to build up their herds.

The announcement was quickly criticized by the cattle industry and GOP lawmakers who said that lowering prices for Americans shouldn’t come at the cost of U.S. ranchers.

“We’re doing it in a very limited fashion because our ranchers can handle it, but our ranchers really needed a little bit of help, and our ranchers want the prices to be down too,” Trump said.

The White House further defended the decision after a report that a Brazilian billionaire influenced it. The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that Trump met with Joesley Batista, who shares control of JBS, the world’s largest meatpacker, a day before the announcement.

Batista and his brother Wesley Batista were fined in 2020 by the Justice Department over charges that they violated the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act by using funds obtained through a bribery scheme to expand operations in the U.S.

The tariff pause also follows the unrelated recall of nearly 30,000 pounds of Argentinian beef that had been distributed in Texas and Florida.

Trump was behind the Resolute Desk on Friday to sign two executive orders, one that allows ranchers and farmers to butcher, process, package and sell their own products and another that requires country-of-origin labeling across all foreign beef.

Trump said the big four processors in the U.S. beef sector — Tyson Foods, JBS S.A., Cargill and National Beef Packing Co. — have a “monopoly” on the industry.

“I’ve heard all about it. I’ve been listening to it … and they say they’re a very nasty group, very difficult to deal with,” he said of the processors. “And they cost our farmers a lot of money, and they cost our ranchers a lot of money, and they cost the public a lot of money in grief, and we’re not going to let it happen any longer.”

When asked about the timeline on the country-of-origin labeling, Trump said he would need to go through Capitol Hill.

“We’re putting it in front of Congress right away,” he said. “It should be no problem.”
