articles.title: He came to Canada to study. Then he protested and was ordered to leave. Gurpreet Singh says the intimidation worked, students are now afraid
articles.summary: US News: Gurpreet Singh thought he was fighting for the right to stay in Canada and build a life after completing his studies. Instead, the 29-year-old Indian .
articles.body: Gurpreet Singh thought he was fighting for the right to stay in Canada and build a life after completing his studies. Instead, the 29-year-old Indian student says his participation in a peaceful protest ended with Canadian immigration authorities ordering him to leave the country. Toronto Star reported that Singh was one of the thousands of protesters who took to the streets after their postgraduate work permit was canceled by Canadian immigration. They all enroled in their courses offered by Portage College, knowing that their course was eligible for a post-completion permit.Singh did not expect the protest to attract the attention of the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).But on August 12, border officials arrived at the demonstration after Calgary police requested immigration-status checks on four people. Singh was among those investigated. He and nine other students have since been issued exclusion orders requiring them to leave Canada and preventing them from returning for a specified period.“They did it to sabotage our protest,” Singh said to Toronto Star.“They are successful in stopping our protest because all the students are afraid now. Nobody is coming out. Everyone is scared CBSA officers would be out there waiting for them.”Singh graduated in 2024, was already working as he was waiting for permitSingh arrived in Canada from India in 2023 on a study permit. He already had a bachelor's degree in English literature from India and initially studied organizational management through a college partnership program in Ontario before moving to Calgary. In December 2024, he graduated from CIOT's administrative professional certificate program and applied for a post-graduation work permit.Then came the refusal.Singh had waited about 18 months for a decision while working at a gas station and later at a concrete plant under maintained status. His application was rejected in early July, shortly after Canada's Immigration Department updated its website to clarify that graduates of certain “non-credit” programs were not eligible for post-graduation work permits.Singh said that it came as a shock because he had enrolled with the understanding that he would be eligible for a work permit after graduating.“I completed my study and they only displayed the non-credit criteria on its website months later,” he said. “It’s just not fair.”His parents spent about $36,000 on his education in Canada, he said.Singh stopped working immediately after losing his authorization on July 9. He subsequently challenged the refusal in Federal Court and was considering ways to maintain his legal status during a 90-day period available to restore his temporary status.Then came the CBSA action at the protest.‘I didn’t have time’Singh says he had been weighing whether to enrol in another program and apply for a new study permit, as some other students had done.“I didn’t have time to do that and now I can’t do anything and must leave Canada,” he said.He is now required to report to CBSA every two weeks and confirm his departure. Having spent his savings on legal fees, Singh says he is relying on community support and crowdfunding.The CBSA says its officers were responding to information supplied by Calgary police. Twenty people at the protest had their immigration status checked; 12 were identified as “possibly inadmissible” and asked to attend follow-up interviews. Advocates say 10 students were ultimately issued exclusion orders.“Inland investigations are an important tool to identify those who should not be in the country and are critical to ensuring compliance with the law,” the CBSA said. “Foreign nationals admitted into Canada are not able to work or study unless authorized and are expected to depart Canada at the end of their authorized period of stay.”The agency also said it recognizes that “the freedom of peaceful assembly is a Charter-protected right.”A protest becomes an immigration caseThe incident has nevertheless triggered a wider debate over whether immigration enforcement was appropriate at a peaceful demonstration.More than 250 civil-liberties, human-rights, labour, migrant and community organizations have endorsed an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and senior federal and provincial officials calling for an independent investigation and the withdrawal of the exclusion orders.“Freedom of expression and peaceful assembly are fundamental Charter-protected rights,” the letter said. “They do not belong only to Canadian citizens or permanent residents. Migrants must be able to speak out, organize and protest without those activities becoming a pathway to immigration enforcement.”Syed Hussan of the Migrant Rights Network, which has supported the students, called the August 12 operation “incredibly dangerous.”“It hearkens to the use of (U.S. President) Trump-style targeting of people for speaking up for their rights,” he said. “It’s completely outside the rules. A protest where you are speaking up for justice should be a place where you get justice, not immigration enforcement.”Julia Sande, a lawyer with Amnesty International Canada, similarly described the action as intimidation.“It’s intimidation, pure and simple,” she said. “Things like freedom of speech, peaceful assembly and the right to protest extend to everyone in Canada. I cannot see how this is seen as relevant or justified to be checking people’s immigration status. It has no bearing on whether they’re allowed to protest.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump has reacted to Maria Bartiromo’s departure from Fox News Media, praising the longtime television anchor as a “true warrior” .
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has reacted to Maria Bartiromo’s departure from Fox News Media, praising the longtime television anchor as a “true warrior” and expressing surprise over the network’s decision to part ways with her.Trump, 80, shared his reaction on Truth Social on Thursday, September 3, shortly after Fox News Media confirmed Bartiromo’s exit. Praising her long-running association with the network, he highlighted her ratings success across multiple programmes.“I can’t believe Maria Bartiromo is no longer going to have her great show(s) on FoxNews/Business,” Trump wrote. “Three different shows, always number one. Maria is a total professional, and a true warrior.”He added, “Her fans, of which there are many, will not be happy. God bless you, Maria!”Maria Bartiromo's long career in financial televisionBartiromo, 58, became a familiar face in financial news long before joining Fox. She first rose to prominence at CNBC, where she hosted programmes including Closing Bell and On the Money with Maria Bartiromo.She joined Fox in 2014 as Fox Business Network’s global markets editor and went on to become one of the network’s most prominent anchors.During her years at Fox, Bartiromo interviewed Trump several times and was also a co-moderator for two debates during the 2016 presidential election cycle.Fox confirms Bartiromo's departureFox News Media announced on Thursday that it had parted ways with Bartiromo, thanking her for her more than 12 years with the company.“We thank Maria for her work over the last 12 ½ years and wish her all the best on her next chapter,” the network said.The company did not provide a reason for the change and said the decision was effective immediately.Bartiromo’s former morning programme is set to transition into Mornings with Fox Business from Friday, September 4. She last appeared on Fox Business Network on August 7 and Fox News on August 9.Her lawyer disputes reports that she was firedWhile Fox described the development as a parting of ways, Bartiromo’s lawyer Bryan Freeman pushed back against reports that she had been fired.“For many years, Maria Bartiromo hosted three number-one-rated television shows on Fox channels. She has been, without question, one of the hardest-working journalists throughout her award-winning career,” Freeman said in a statement.He denied reports that Bartiromo had been fired and maintained that she remains an employee of Fox.Meanwhile, Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street is being renamed FBN’s Wall Street. Cheryl Casone will host the programme when it returns, with rotating anchors expected to take over thereafter.Fox announces further programming changesBartiromo’s departure comes as Fox prepares to make additional changes to its weekday programming schedule. The network is expected to announce a new Fox Business Network lineup in the coming weeks.Fox News Channel’s Sunday Morning Futures will also have Jason Chaffetz as host on Sunday, September 6, with a permanent new host to be announced later.The latest shake-up follows other high-profile exits from Fox. articles.title: Watchdog report alleges misconduct by Trump’s former labour secretary
articles.summary: Lori Chavez-DeRemer reportedly used staff for personal tasks, drank at work and violated ethics regulations.
articles.body:
A federal watchdog in the United States has published a report detailing allegations of misconduct involving former US Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer , who resigned in April.

On Thursday night, the Department of Labor’s Office of Inspector General released 44 pages detailing incidents where Chavez-DeRemer reportedly blurred the line between her public office and personal life.

The report drew from 500 documents and interviews with 53 current and former Labor Department employees, as well as one employee from another federal agency.

It said 38 of the interviewees described the secretary’s office as a “toxic, intimidating and humiliating” workplace.

It also accuses Chavez-DeRemer of using government employees for private errands, drinking alcohol in her office during working hours and developing an “inappropriate relationship” with a member of her security detail.

The rumours of misconduct ultimately forced Chavez-DeRemer to leave her post on April 20.

She became the third cabinet secretary to leave the second administration of President Donald Trump, after the departures of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Attorney General Pam Bondi earlier this year.

Chavez-DeRemer, a former Republican Congress member from Oregon, was sworn in on March 11, 2025. Her position lasted just over a year.

The final months of her tenure saw the resignations of several high-level staff members. One, Melissa Robey, claimed in media reports that she was fired under pressure from the White House after sitting down with the inspector general’s office.

Thursday’s report alleged that Chavez-DeRemer oversaw a hostile workplace, with senior staff having “routinely engaged in threatening, demeaning, and abusive verbal and written communication” towards their colleagues.

It cited incidents of Labor Department employees being berated in front of colleagues and threatened with termination.

Some of the episodes involved Chavez-DeRemer’s chief of staff, Rebecca Wright. She allegedly relocated one employee’s desk to avoid having a “fat person” seen in the front office, and she reportedly advised another employee not to cut her hair too short to avoid looking like a “lesbian”.

The report alleges that Chavez-DeRemer was aware of such incidents but failed to take action to prevent them from happening.

Investigators also found that Chavez-DeRemer herself directed government employees to perform personal tasks during official time.

A personal aide and executive assistant were reportedly sent to her residence to organise her closet, hang laundry and arrange her clothing and purses.

Investigators said another employee, who was Hispanic, was directed to oversee workers at Chavez-DeRemer’s home, including a moving crew.

Employees were also tasked with buying personal items, including gifts, picture frames, holiday decorations and alcohol, according to the report.

Chavez-DeRemer, Wright and her deputy chief of staff also regularly drank alcohol in the secretary’s study during duty hours, according to witness reports. Some employees said they felt pressured or ridiculed when they declined to participate.

Department of Labor policy requires advance written authorisation for alcohol on federal property. Investigators found no record that the required approval had been obtained.

The watchdog also zeroed in on aspects of Chavez-DeRemer’s personal behaviour that violated government ethics standards.

Regulations prohibit government employees from using their office “to coerce or induce another person, including a subordinate, to provide” them with “any financial or other benefit”.

It also bars officials from requesting subordinates to use government time for activities that fall outside their job’s official duties.

But the report determined that Chavez-DeRemer developed an “inappropriately close and unprofessional” relationship with a senior agent on her protective detail.

Witnesses reported seeing Chavez-DeRemer massaging the agent’s shoulder, golfing and gambling with him, and leaving an event walking arm-in-arm.

The report, however, did not find “sufficient” evidence to conclude the relationship was sexual.

Still, investigators documented conduct where the relationship between Chavez-DeRemer and the agent created conflicts of interest or inappropriate work situations.

The report describes an April 2025 incident in which Chavez-DeRemer was taking a personal trip to Oregon and asked her security detail to make an off-the-record stop at a club featuring partially nude dancers.

The senior agent she was involved with was also on the trip. A limousine driver objected to her requests to drop money onto a performer, but the senior agent reportedly instructed him to comply.

The agent occasionally reduced the number of officers covering Chavez-DeRemer or assumed sole responsibility for her protection.

Investigators obtained electronic hotel door lock records suggesting the two spent time overnight in each other’s rooms and reviewed video footage that documented his visits to her home.

The report also found travel policy violations involving excessive spending.

In November 2025, for instance, Chavez-DeRemer and two other officials reportedly stayed at hotels in Palm Beach, Florida, to attend an America First Policy Institute gala.

The cost for their lodging approached or exceeded three times the government reimbursement rate, despite there being no documentation showing the required approval for the increased costs.

Investigators further found that Chavez-DeRemer failed to report several gifts to the government, including rodeo tickets, an alligator-hide wallet and cowboy hats given to her and her husband.

Federal government officials are required to report gifts they receive as part of their official duties, to avoid conflicts of interest.

In its conclusion, the watchdog report recommends structural changes to the Labor Department, including removing the protective units from the secretary’s oversight.

Such agents, it suggested, could instead work under the inspector general’s office.

The report also called for independent travel audits, stronger whistleblower protections and annual training for senior leaders.

Since resigning her cabinet post, Chavez-DeRemer has announced she has taken up a senior adviser position at Think Big, a public affairs firm.

According to the company’s website, the former secretary heads a practice dedicated to labour and national infrastructure.

articles.title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
articles.summary: With Argentina's President Milei promising "winds of change" over the Falklands, will Donald Trump shift his stance on British rule?
articles.body:
The tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week.

It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer.

President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands.

The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details: the islands – over which the European powers had interchanged control throughout the 17th and 18th centuries – were uninhabited at the time the British reoccupied the land. The Argentine settlement had been forced out two years earlier, not by the British but by the Americans. A warship, the USS Lexington, destroyed a fort established there in December 1831 amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights.

Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so.

"Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands.

That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982 – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.

For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran.

"You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.

Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his former vice-president, Victoria Villarroel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.

Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.

With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.

In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the 'Don-roe Doctrine', a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.

Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.

Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".
